items.title: What Does the Penguin Scene Mean in 'Fight Club'?
items.summary: I feel like I have seen David Fincher's Fight Club many times, yet. Every time I put it on, I'm surprised by the penguin scene. It sort of comes out of nowhere, and I do a double-take as I try to figure out why Edward Norton is standing across from an Emperor Penguin and why it's talking to him. It happens in this imaginary "power cave" when he finds his inner animal, and that penguin says one word to him: "Slide." Yeah, it's one of those scenes that you kind of want to Google right after you see it to figure out what the heck is going on. Well, this time, that's what I did, and I want to bring the answer to you. Here is why that scene works so well and what it actually means. Let's dive in together. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The "Power Animal" Joke The power of the scene is that his inner animals aren't something fierce, but something inherently goofy. And it fits his personality in its fake, dressed-up fur, as he dresses for work, and it's harmless and goofy. This is a mirror of how he thinks of himself and what he wants to change his animal into. It could also be a visual plant, because later we see Tyler donning fur, like he's the predator our guy wants to be (and is). The Slippery Slope When the penguin says "Slide," Norton doesn't question it; he just follows its lead. Then he slides right into Marla Singer (Helena Bonham Carter). Again, visually, you could see his slippery-slope downfall as he smashes into someone who will affect his life moving forward. Also, this is a guy who just slides through life, and he finally needs to take conscious steps instead of following the path of least resistance. The Mental State Fincher builds the ice cave to match the Narrator's mental state and the story's themes, so we can really understand what the narrator is going through. This is a cold place that will soon be replaced by the heat of fighting and blowing things up. The Bottom Line David Fincher does everything on purpose. items.title: The Ending of 'Evil Dead Burn' Explained
items.summary: Evil Dead Burn is the sixth theatrical installment in the iconic Evil Dead franchise, a horror series that is growing increasingly complicated. While 2023’s Evil Dead Rise was a standalone sequel that largely ignored the continuities of the original trilogy and the 2013 remake (instead simply taking place in the same universe), that movie introduced a number of characters and storylines that have echoes in Evil Dead Burn, which debuted this summer. While we wait to see what the upcoming 2028 sequel Evil Dead Wrath brings to the franchise, let’s break down what happened at the end of Evil Dead Burn so we can be properly prepared. The Plot of Evil Dead Burn Naturally, in order to understand the ending of Evil Dead Burn, we need to make sure we have a handle on the beginning. The movie, which was directed by Sébastien Vaniček (who co-wrote the screenplay with his Infested collaborator Florent Bernard), establishes many different plot points following different family members in an order that might seem slightly confusing at first, but we’ll lay it out plainly here. The whole movie revolves around the Price family and the complicated relationships that connect and ultimately destroy them. The first of these relationships is introduced immediately as Joseph Price (Wednesday’s Hunter Doohan) searches through the archives of his late grandfather, whose association with the secret society The Circle of the Wise Men led him to be estranged from the rest of his family. It also allowed him to take possession of the Kandarian Dagger, a weapon with the power to destroy Kandarian demons (who, when they possess the bodies of humans, are called Deadites). The sheer power of the weapon attracts Deadites, who want the Dagger destroyed, so when Joseph unsheaths it, it awakens Evil Dead Rise’s Deadite Jessica (Greta Van Den Brink, the stunt performer who portrayed the Deadite version of the character, who was primarily portrayed by Anna-Maree Thomas in Rise). items.title: This New 30mm f/2.4 Lens Aims to Expand the Range of Your Medium Format Cameras
items.summary: While more tailored to the needs of medium-format photographers, this new Pittura 30mm f/2.4 from Zhong Yi Optics could be an interesting option for medium-format videographers and hybrid content creators looking for a unique wide-angle prime for their various shooting needs. Designed specifically for high-res medium-format shooting, this Zhong Yi Pittura 30mm f/2.4 looks quite capable across a range of shot types and comes with native mount options for Hasselblad XCD or your Fujifilm GFX camera systems. Let’s check it out. The Zhong Yi Pittura 30mm f/2.4 Prime Lens The latest from Zhong Yi Optics, the Pittura 30mm f/2.4 is fast, compact, and wide, and ready for medium-format systems. Designed as a portable wide-angle lens for a range of uses, the lens seems primarily aimed at bridging the gap between extreme light-gathering capabilities and close-quarters versatility. From the look of the sample photos, the lens sure looks capable of delivering a distinct, painterly optical signature that showcases a solid range of dramatic depth and overall rich character for your high-megapixel captures. Ideal for any medium-format camera system, the Zhong Yi Pittura 30mm f/2.4 is specifically tailored for Hasselblad XCD or Fujifilm GFX camera lineups, which should make it appealing to video pros, photo pros, or any other type of combo creator. Price and Availability The new Zhong Yi Pittura 30mm f/2.4 Prime Lens is live on the company’s website, where it is set to retail for $499 beginning today. You can find the full specs and purchase link below. items.title: Hollywood Throwback: The Story Behind Indiana Jones’ Hat
items.summary: My favorite character of all time is Indiana Jones. At my core, I am a sucker for adventure movies that keep you on the edge of your seat, and from the time I was 5 all the way through now, that's the one guy I'd like to trade places with in the mythical movie world. The thing about Indy is that it's not just his personality, but he exudes this coolness from his costume, too. The jacket. The whip. The fedora. They all make up the man. Well, what's the story behind the getup? And where did Indy get that hat? Today, we're going to dig into the legend of Indiana Jones and talk about how one of the best-written characters ever came to be. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Character Indiana Jones was created by George Lucas and Steven Spielberg on their hunt for a protagonist who could be an homage to the adventure movies they grew up loving. Funnily enough, the character was named Indiana after Lucas's dog. But Jones came later, when Spielberg didn't like the name Indiana Smith. From there, the two of them began brainstorming the life and look of this icon. Along with Lawrence Kasdan, the auteurs looked for inspiration from Charlton Heston in Secret of the Incas (1954) and Humphrey Bogart in The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (1948). Once the screenplay was written by Kasdan, and they eventually cast Harrison Ford (after Tom Selleck was forced to do Magnum PI by CBS), costume designer Deborah Nadoolman Landis took Harrison Ford to the famous Bermans & Nathans costume house in London to test out a few different looks. The Herbert Johnson "Australian" The idea was to find a hat that complemented Ford’s facial features while remaining striking in high-contrast lighting, which Spielberg knew he wanted to use to hark back to the serials of old. They needed something to really tie together the man and the movie star, so they ultimately turned to the historic London hatter Herbert Johnson.
